Before we start

What your business needs in place.

Internal systems fail on organisation, not on code. These are the parts only you can supply.

A sponsor with authority

Someone senior enough to settle a disagreement between two departments. Internal systems die when nobody can decide whose process wins, and no amount of engineering fixes that.

The process as it actually runs

Including the spreadsheet somebody keeps on the side and the step everyone skips. Building the documented process rather than the real one is the classic way an internal system goes unused.

Access to the systems that hold the data

ERP, HR, finance, the old database. Read access and a test environment at minimum, and the name of whoever administers each one.

Time from the people who will use it

A few hours from two or three real users, early. Systems designed only with management input get built correctly and used reluctantly.

A decision on data residency

Where the data may physically live, and who may see it. In Saudi and Egypt this is often decided for you by the sector, and it changes the architecture — so it is settled before, not after.

What you send

The handover, in one list.

Send it in one go and the clock starts.

  • The process, written or drawn, however roughly
  • Who does what, and who approves what
  • Sample data or real forms — even photographs of paper ones
  • Access to the systems it must read from or write to
  • Any compliance rules that constrain the design
  • Roughly how many people will use it, and from where

How it runs

Six steps, and you see each one.

  1. 01

    Map

    Sit with the people doing the work and record the process as it really runs, including the workarounds.

  2. 02

    Blueprint

    Modules, data model, integrations and build order, written down and priced.

  3. 03

    First module

    The one that pays back fastest goes to production first, with real users on it.

  4. 04

    Integrate

    Wire it to the systems that already hold the truth, so nobody types anything twice.

  5. 05

    Stage by stage

    Each module usable before the next begins. You can stop at any stage and still have something working.

  6. 06

    Handover

    Documentation, environment access and training for whoever maintains it. Then the Care plan, or your team.

Scope

What this is not, and who it is not for.

These are quoted separately, so the price above stays a price.

  • Licences for ERP, database or BI products
  • Hardware and infrastructure procurement
  • Business process consulting beyond what the build needs
  • Data entry and historical data cleaning
  • Training beyond the handover sessions
  • Regulatory certification and audit sign-off

Right fit, wrong fit

Saves a call that would end in no.

A good fit

  • A process runs on spreadsheets and email and has outgrown both
  • Two systems hold the same data and disagree
  • You need an audit trail because someone will ask
  • You want it staged, not one irreversible commitment
  • Arabic interfaces and RTL are a requirement, not a nice-to-have

Not a fit

  • Nobody senior is willing to own the decisions
  • You want a product demo rather than a build
  • An off-the-shelf product would obviously do the job — I will tell you if it would
  • The requirement is a certification, not a system

After launch

After handover.

An internal system without an owner degrades quietly: reports stop matching, an integration silently fails, nobody updates the dependency with the security advisory. The Care plan puts a named engineer on it who already knows the design.

Questions

The ones people actually ask.

Should we build or buy?

Buy, whenever something off the shelf fits — I will say so, and the discovery is where that comes out. Building is right when the process is genuinely yours, when integration is the hard part, or when licence cost per user outgrows the build inside two years.

Can you work with our existing team?

Yes, and it is usually the better arrangement. I take the architecture and the hard parts, your developers take the volume, and the handover happens continuously instead of at the end.

How do you price something this open-ended?

Discovery is fixed. Each module after it is fixed against its own written scope. You are never asked to commit to the whole programme up front, and you can stop after any stage with something that works.

What about our data leaving the country?

It does not have to. The architecture follows your residency rules — on-premise, a local region, or a hybrid where only what is allowed to leave leaves. Decide it before the design, not after.

Who maintains it when you are gone?

Your team, if you have one — the handover is documentation, walkthroughs and access, not a zip file. If you do not have one, the Care plan covers it until you do.
